narrative:
The model estimated a 60% chance you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, meaning the admissions decision treated failure as more likely than success. That probability is why your application was denied; it reflects academic indicators that raised concern, not a judgment about your ability.

The strongest factor was your undergraduate GPA of 2.20, far below the 3.23 average among accepted students, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 31 was the second most influential factor, also below the accepted average of about 37, and it likewise increased the estimated risk. The third factor, your third-year class decile of 5, was slightly more favorable than the accepted average of about 5.79 and pushed modestly toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the two academic signals. Your first-year decile matched the accepted average, while family income and full-time status did not drive this explanation.

To improve a future application, focus on the areas weighted most heavily. Consider retaking the LSAT after structured preparation, and strengthen your academic record through additional rigorous coursework or a post-baccalaureate program if feasible. Seek admissions advising, apply to a balanced range of schools, and ask whether you can submit an addendum explaining any context behind the GPA or LSAT. A stronger retake or stronger recent coursework would most directly change the picture.
